passage: In the college learning centre, Mahima, a third-year, sat with junior Vandana over a statistics sheet. Mahima had scored well last year and explained mean and spread easily. Then Vandana asked, "Why do we square the differences?" Mahima opened her mouth and found nothing. She had always just done it. "Give me till tomorrow," she said, and felt her ears go hot. That night she reread the chapter, drew a number line, and tried explaining aloud to the wall. The next day she showed Vandana that squaring stops plus and minus from cancelling out. Vandana wrote it down. "Thanks," Mahima said. "You made me learn it properly."

qa.q: What question did Vandana ask that Mahima could not answer?
qa.a: Vandana asked, "Why do we square the differences?"

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling when her ears went hot?
qa.a: Embarrassed, having realised she had only ever done it out of habit.

qa.q: What did Mahima do to fill the gap in her understanding?
qa.a: She reread the chapter, drew a number line, explained aloud to the wall and returned the next day with the reason.

qa.q: How might Vandana have seen Mahima's "Give me till tomorrow"?
qa.a: As honest and trustworthy, since Mahima came back the next day with a real answer.

grounding: Shows a student tutor finding a gap in her own understanding through a junior's question and fixing it.

passage:
Dear Alka,
You once told me the best way to learn something is to teach it, and I laughed. This month I've been tutoring a first-year in programming, and you were right. On Tuesday she asked why a function can call itself without going on forever. I said, "Because of the base case," and she said, "But what is that doing?" I had no answer beyond the words. That night I traced a small example on paper, step by step, then explained it to my flatmate's cat. On Thursday I showed her, and she said, "Oh, it stops at zero!" I now keep a page in my notebook called "Questions I couldn't answer". It is already my most useful page.
Naveen

qa.q: What did the first-year ask on Tuesday?
qa.a: The first-year asked why a function can call itself without going on forever.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling when the first-year asked "But what is that doing?"
qa.a: Caught out and uneasy, since Naveen had the words but no real reason behind them.

qa.q: What did Naveen do to close the gap before Thursday?
qa.a: Naveen traced a small example on paper step by step and explained it aloud, then showed the first-year.

qa.q: What might it be like for the first-year to ask a hard question and get a clear answer two days later?
qa.a: Satisfying and encouraging, since the first-year went from confusion to "Oh, it stops at zero!" 🙂

grounding: Shows a student tutor whose learner's questions expose gaps in the tutor's own understanding, driving a clearer explanation.

passage:
Dear Mrs Fernandes,
You once told our class that the best way to learn physics was to teach it. I thought that was something teachers say. This term I found out you were right.
I'm tutoring a first-year student, Omkar, twice a week. In the first session he asked why a heavier ball and a lighter ball fall at the same speed. I started to answer and realised I only knew the rule, not the reason. I said, "Let me come back to you." My face was hot the whole way home.
I spent that weekend with my old notes and the textbook, working it through until I could say it simply. Next session I explained it with two bottles, one full and one empty. Omkar got it, and so, honestly, did I.
Every week he finds another hole in what I thought I knew. It is humbling and oddly fun.
With thanks,
Bhavna

qa.q: How often does Bhavna tutor Omkar?
qa.a: Twice a week.

qa.q: How did Bhavna feel on the way home after the first session?
qa.a: Bhavna felt embarrassed, face hot the whole way home, after realising only the rule was known and not the reason.

qa.q: What did Bhavna do well after finding the gap?
qa.a: Bhavna admitted it, said "Let me come back to you," worked it through over the weekend and returned with a clear, tested example.

qa.q: How might Omkar see Bhavna's honest "Let me come back to you"?
qa.a: Omkar would likely trust Bhavna more, since the next session brought a clear answer instead of a bluff.

grounding: Illustrates a student tutor whose junior's questions expose gaps in the tutor's own understanding, making teaching a way to learn.

passage:
You asked on this show what surprised me about tutoring. I'm Ayesha, second-year economics, and it's this: my tutee taught me more than I taught him.
Karthik is in first year. We were doing basic statistics, and I was feeling pretty clever. Then he asked, "Why do we divide by n minus one for the sample and not by n?"
I opened my mouth, and nothing came. I had been doing it for a year. I had never asked why. I said, "Good question, let's both find out," which was really me buying time.
That night I read three explanations and tried each one on my roommate. The first two confused her. The third one, about using up one piece of information on the mean, finally made sense to both of us.
Next session I explained it in two minutes. Karthik nodded, then explained it back to me in his own words. That's when I knew I really had it, too.

qa.q: What did Karthik ask about dividing?
qa.a: "Why do we divide by n minus one for the sample and not by n?"

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling when nothing came?
qa.a: Ayesha felt caught out and a little embarrassed after feeling clever, realising the reason had never been asked.

qa.q: How did Ayesha test the explanation before the next session?
qa.a: Ayesha tried three explanations on the roommate and kept the one that made sense to both.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel when Ayesha said "let's both find out"?
qa.a: Karthik probably felt respected and curious rather than foolish, since his question was treated as a good one.

grounding: Shows a student tutor whose junior's question exposes a gap, and who learns more by preparing a clear, tested explanation.

passage:
Week one. Sunaina started tutoring Thomas, a first-year student, in accounting at the college's peer-help desk. She raced through journal entries. He wrote everything down. She walked home feeling useful.
Week two. Thomas asked, "Why does depreciation go on the expense side if no money actually leaves?" Sunaina started, stopped, started again. She could do the entries in her sleep, but she could not explain the idea. "I'll tell you next week," she said, and felt her ears burn.
That weekend she sat with her old textbook, then with a notebook, writing the answer in her own words. She tested it on her younger brother, who knew nothing about accounts. He got it on the third version.
Week three. She walked in with a pencil and a story about a delivery van losing value every year. Thomas asked two follow-up questions, and this time she could answer both. On the way out, she realised she understood depreciation properly for the first time.

qa.q: Where did Sunaina tutor Thomas?
qa.a: At the college's peer-help desk.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel when she could not explain depreciation?
qa.a: Sunaina felt embarrassed and caught out; her ears burned as she promised to answer next week.

qa.q: What did Sunaina do that turned the gap into learning?
qa.a: Sunaina wrote the answer in her own words and tested it on her younger brother until it made sense to someone new.

qa.q: How might Thomas see Sunaina in week three?
qa.a: Thomas would likely feel she is more trustworthy, since she came back with a clear story and answered his follow-up questions.

grounding: Illustrates a student tutor who discovers gaps in her own understanding through a junior's questions and learns by preparing a clear explanation.

passage: Avni, you asked why I still keep that old chemistry notebook. At nineteen, in my second year of college, I tutored a first-year boy, Karthik, in organic chemistry. I thought I knew it cold; I had topped the paper. In the first week he asked, "But why does the electron move this way and not that way?" I opened my mouth and nothing came. I had memorised the arrows, never the reason. That night I sat up with my textbook, the way I should have done in first year. Every Tuesday he brought a new "but why", and every Tuesday I found another hole in my own head. So I started writing each explanation in this notebook before our sessions and testing it on my roommate first. By the end of term Karthik passed well, and honestly, so did my own understanding. Your Farida Khala learned more from those Tuesdays than from any lecture.

qa.q: What did Farida do before each session with Karthik?
qa.a: She wrote each explanation in her notebook and tested it on her roommate first.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling when Karthik first asked why the electron moves that way?
qa.a: Farida felt caught out and embarrassed, because she had topped the paper yet found she had memorised the arrows without knowing the reason.

qa.q: Which choice in the story turned Farida's weak spot into real understanding?
qa.a: Sitting up with the textbook to find the reason, then writing and testing each explanation before sessions, turned every question into a chance to fill a gap.

qa.q: How might Karthik have experienced being tutored by Farida?
qa.a: Karthik had a tutor who took his "but why" questions seriously and came back with clearer answers each week, which helped him pass well.

grounding: Shows a student tutoring a junior and finding gaps in their own understanding as the junior's questions arrive.
